claim: Zinc and copper are involved in neuronal differentiation and synaptic plasticity.
source: Zinc and copper are involved in neuronal differentiation and synaptic plasticity but the molecular mechanisms behind these processes are still elusive due in part to the difficulty of imaging trace metals together with proteins at the synaptic level.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature establishing these roles.

claim: The molecular mechanisms behind zinc and copper involvement in neuronal differentiation and synaptic plasticity are still elusive.
source: Zinc and copper are involved in neuronal differentiation and synaptic plasticity but the molecular mechanisms behind these processes are still elusive due in part to the difficulty of imaging trace metals together with proteins at the synaptic level.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The difficulty of imaging trace metals together with proteins at the synaptic level contributes to the elusiveness of molecular mechanisms.
source: Zinc and copper are involved in neuronal differentiation and synaptic plasticity but the molecular mechanisms behind these processes are still elusive due in part to the difficulty of imaging trace metals together with proteins at the synaptic level.
evidence: This is an inference about why the mechanisms remain elusive.

claim: Stimulated-emission-depletion microscopy and synchrotron X-ray fluorescence imaging were both performed with 40 nm spatial resolution.
source: We correlate stimulated-emission-depletion microscopy of proteins and synchrotron X-ray fluorescence imaging of trace metals, both performed with 40 nm spatial resolution, on primary rat hippocampal neurons.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the spatial resolution achieved in the experiments.

claim: The study was performed on primary rat hippocampal neurons.
source: We correlate stimulated-emission-depletion microscopy of proteins and synchrotron X-ray fluorescence imaging of trace metals, both performed with 40 nm spatial resolution, on primary rat hippocampal neurons.
evidence: This describes the biological sample used in the study.

claim: Zinc and tubulin co-localize at the nanoscale in dendrites.
source: We reveal the co-localization at the nanoscale of zinc and tubulin in dendrites with a molecular ratio of about one zinc atom per tubulin-αβ dimer.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the correlative imaging experiments.

claim: The molecular ratio of zinc to tubulin-αβ dimer is about one zinc atom per tubulin-αβ dimer.
source: We reveal the co-localization at the nanoscale of zinc and tubulin in dendrites with a molecular ratio of about one zinc atom per tubulin-αβ dimer.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the nano-SXRF analysis.

claim: Copper and F-actin co-segregate within the nano-architecture of dendritic protrusions.
source: We observe the co-segregation of copper and F-actin within the nano-architecture of dendritic protrusions.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the correlative imaging experiments.

claim: Zinc chelation causes a decrease in the expression of cytoskeleton proteins in dendrites and spines.
source: In addition, zinc chelation causes a decrease in the expression of cytoskeleton proteins in dendrites and spines.
evidence: This is a finding from the TPEN exposure experiments.

claim: Zinc and copper have new functions in the modulation of the cytoskeleton morphology in dendrites.
source: Overall, these results indicate new functions for zinc and copper in the modulation of the cytoskeleton morphology in dendrites, a mechanism associated to neuronal plasticity and memory formation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the combined findings from the study.

claim: The modulation of cytoskeleton morphology in dendrites is a mechanism associated with neuronal plasticity and memory formation.
source: Overall, these results indicate new functions for zinc and copper in the modulation of the cytoskeleton morphology in dendrites, a mechanism associated to neuronal plasticity and memory formation.
evidence: This connects the findings to established knowledge about neuronal plasticity.

claim: Zinc ions are stored in pre-synaptic vesicles in a subset of glutamatergic neurons.
source: Zinc ions are stored in pre-synaptic vesicles in a subset of glutamatergic neurons.
evidence: This is established knowledge about zinc localization in neurons.

claim: Zinc ions are released in the synaptic cleft during neurotransmission.
source: They are released in the synaptic cleft during neurotransmission.
evidence: This is established knowledge about zinc function in synaptic transmission.

claim: Zinc ions are effectors of synaptic plasticity by modulating the activity of neurotransmitter receptors such as NMDA and AMPA receptors.
source: Zinc ions are effectors of synaptic plasticity by modulating the activity of neurotransmitter receptors such as NMDA (N-methyl-d-aspartate) and AMPA (α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid) receptors (NMDARs and AMPARs) (Vergnano et al., 2014; Barr and Burdette, 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The role of copper in neural functions is less well described than that of zinc.
source: The role of copper in neural functions is less well described than that of zinc, but copper ions are also known to be released in the synaptic cleft where they can modulate the activity of neurotransmitter receptors (D'Ambrosi and Rossi, 2015).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Copper ions are released in the synaptic cleft where they can modulate the activity of neurotransmitter receptors.
source: The role of copper in neural functions is less well described than that of zinc, but copper ions are also known to be released in the synaptic cleft where they can modulate the activity of neurotransmitter receptors (D'Ambrosi and Rossi, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Copper is involved in the regulation of spontaneous neuronal activity.
source: Copper is involved in broad neuronal functions such as the regulation of spontaneous neuronal activity or of rest–activity cycles (Chang, 2015; Xiao et al., 2018), and more generally in neuronal differentiation (Hatori et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Copper is involved in the regulation of rest-activity cycles.
source: Copper is involved in broad neuronal functions such as the regulation of spontaneous neuronal activity or of rest–activity cycles (Chang, 2015; Xiao et al., 2018), and more generally in neuronal differentiation (Hatori et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Copper is involved in neuronal differentiation.
source: Copper is involved in broad neuronal functions such as the regulation of spontaneous neuronal activity or of rest–activity cycles (Chang, 2015; Xiao et al., 2018), and more generally in neuronal differentiation (Hatori et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Copper and zinc could be involved in the structure of dendrites and dendritic spines.
source: In addition to these functions of the labile fraction of metals on neuronal signaling and differentiation, we have recently indicated that copper and zinc could be involved in the structure of dendrites and dendritic spines (Perrin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a prior finding from the authors' previous work.

claim: Zinc localizes all along dendritic shafts in cultured hippocampal neurons.
source: We have shown on cultured hippocampal neurons the localization of zinc all along dendritic shafts and that of copper in the neck of dendritic spines, suggesting their interaction with cytoskeleton proteins.
evidence: This is a prior finding from the authors' previous work.

claim: Copper localizes in the neck of dendritic spines in cultured hippocampal neurons.
source: We have shown on cultured hippocampal neurons the localization of zinc all along dendritic shafts and that of copper in the neck of dendritic spines, suggesting their interaction with cytoskeleton proteins.
evidence: This is a prior finding from the authors' previous work.

claim: The localization of zinc along dendritic shafts and copper in the neck of dendritic spines suggests their interaction with cytoskeleton proteins.
source: We have shown on cultured hippocampal neurons the localization of zinc all along dendritic shafts and that of copper in the neck of dendritic spines, suggesting their interaction with cytoskeleton proteins.
evidence: This is an inference from prior observations.

claim: Understanding the functions of copper and zinc in the cytoskeleton structure requires correlating metal localization with relevant cytoskeleton proteins at the sub-dendritic level.
source: Understanding the functions of copper and zinc in the cytoskeleton structure would require however to correlate metal localization with respect to relevant cytoskeleton proteins at the sub-dendritic level.
evidence: This is a statement about the methodological requirements for the study.

claim: Nano-SXRF imaging using hard X-ray beams above 10 keV energy allows mapping of element distributions in single cells with high analytical sensitivity.
source: Nano-Synchrotron X-Ray Fluorescence (Nano-SXRF) imaging using hard X-ray beams, typically above 10 keV energy, is a powerful technique to investigate the cellular localization of metals since it allows the mapping of element distributions in single cells with high analytical sensitivity (Victor et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the capabilities of nano-SXRF.

claim: SXRF has reached a spatial resolution of 13 nm on ID16A beamline at ESRF using Kirkpatrick-Baez focusing mirrors.
source: Using Kirkpatrick–Baez (KB) focusing mirrors, SXRF has reached a spatial resolution of 13 nm on ID16A beamline at the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility (ESRF), while maintaining a high photon flux as required for detecting trace elements (da Silva et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a technical specification of the beamline capabilities supported by citation.

claim: A correlative microscopy approach consisting of labeling organelles or proteins with specific fluorophores for live-cell imaging prior to SXRF imaging has been previously reported.
source: We have previously reported a correlative microscopy approach consisting in labeling organelles or proteins with specific fluorophores for live-cell imaging prior to SXRF imaging (Roudeau et al., 2014; Carmona et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes prior work by the authors.

claim: The previous correlative approach is limited by the spatial resolution of optical fluorescence microscopy, above 200 nm.
source: This correlative approach is limited by the spatial resolution of optical fluorescence microscopy, above 200 nm, which is larger than the spatial resolution achieved today with nano-SXRF and insufficient to resolve synaptic sub-structures.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of conventional fluorescence microscopy.

claim: The spatial resolution of optical fluorescence microscopy (above 200 nm) is larger than the spatial resolution achieved with nano-SXRF.
source: This correlative approach is limited by the spatial resolution of optical fluorescence microscopy, above 200 nm, which is larger than the spatial resolution achieved today with nano-SXRF and insufficient to resolve synaptic sub-structures.
evidence: This is a comparison of technical capabilities.

claim: The spatial resolution of optical fluorescence microscopy is insufficient to resolve synaptic sub-structures.
source: This correlative approach is limited by the spatial resolution of optical fluorescence microscopy, above 200 nm, which is larger than the spatial resolution achieved today with nano-SXRF and insufficient to resolve synaptic sub-structures.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of conventional fluorescence microscopy for the specific application.

claim: The study presents a method to correlate nano-SXRF with STED performed both at 40 nm resolution.
source: To overcome this limitation we present a method to correlate nano-SXRF with STED (STimulated-Emission-Depletion microscopy) performed both at 40 nm resolution.
evidence: This is a description of the methodological contribution of the study.

claim: The combination of STED and nano-SXRF enables observation of trace metals co-localization with cytoskeleton proteins at the synaptic level in rat hippocampal neurons.
source: With the combination of these two high-resolution imaging techniques we observe trace metals co-localization with cytoskeleton proteins at the synaptic level in rat hippocampal neurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding enabled by the correlative imaging method.

claim: The study explored the effect of zinc deficiency induced by TPEN on the expression of cytoskeleton proteins in dendrites and dendritic spines.
source: Furthermore, we explored the effect of zinc deficiency induced by TPEN, an intracellular zinc-chelator, on the expression of cytoskeleton proteins in dendrites and dendritic spines.
evidence: This describes an experimental approach used in the study.

claim: Primary rat hippocampal neurons were cultured in vitro during 15 days (DIV15) on sterile silicon nitride membranes placed above an astrocyte feeder layer.
source: Primary rat hippocampal neurons were cultured in vitro during 15 days (DIV15) on sterile SN membranes placed above an astrocyte feeder layer as adapted from Kaech and Banker, 2006; Perrin et al., 2015.
evidence: This describes the cell culture methodology.

claim: Silicon nitride membranes with an orientation frame were used to facilitate reproducible positioning of samples during correlative imaging.
source: SN membranes with an orientation frame were used to facilitate the reproducible positioning of the samples during the correlative imaging procedure (Figure 1a).
evidence: This describes a methodological feature of the sample preparation.

claim: Silicon nitride membranes are biocompatible, trace metal free, 500 nm thin, transparent, flat and rigid supports developed for X-ray microscopy.
source: SN membranes are biocompatible, trace metal free, 500 nm thin, transparent, flat and rigid supports developed for X-ray microscopy.
evidence: This describes the properties of the substrate used.

claim: DIV15 primary rat hippocampal neurons were stained with either SiR-actin, SiR-tubulin, or with SiR-tubulin and SiR700-actin together for STED microscopy.
source: To perform STED microscopy we stained the DIV15 primary rat hippocampal neurons with either SiR-actin, SiR-tubulin, or with SiR-tubulin and SiR700-actin together.
evidence: This describes the labeling methodology.

claim: SiR-based fluorophores are based on the actin ligand jasplakinolide and the tubulin ligand docetaxel.
source: These two far-red SiR-based fluorophores have been developed for live-cell super-resolution microscopy and are based respectively on the actin ligand jasplakinolide and the tubulin ligand docetaxel (Lukinavičius et al., 2014; Lukinavičius et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the fluorophores supported by citations.

claim: SiR-based fluorescent dyes are suitable for STED imaging and do not require overexpression of proteins.
source: On the one hand, they are markers suitable for STED imaging that do not require overexpression of the proteins.
evidence: This describes an advantage of the chosen fluorophores.

claim: SiR-based fluorescent dyes block the cell structure when bound to cytoskeleton proteins, preventing movement of regions of interest between live-cell STED imaging and cryofixation.
source: On the other hand, when these molecules bind to proteins of the cytoskeleton they block the cell structure preventing movement of the regions of interest in the time span between living cells STED imaging and cryofixation.
evidence: This describes a functional property of the fluorophores important for the correlative imaging approach.

claim: STED images were recorded at 40 nm spatial resolution.
source: STED images were recorded at 40 nm spatial resolution.
evidence: This is a technical specification of the imaging method.

claim: Silicon nitride membranes were plunge-frozen at −165°C and freeze-dried at −90°C under secondary vacuum before analysis on ID16A beamline.
source: Then the SN membranes were plunge-frozen at −165°C and freeze-dried at −90°C under secondary vacuum before analysis on ID16A beamline at ESRF (Figure 1b).
evidence: This describes the sample preparation protocol.

claim: Nano-SXRF and synchrotron X-ray phase contrast imaging were performed with an X-ray beam size of 40 nm at 17 KeV energy.
source: Nano-SXRF and synchrotron X-ray phase contrast imaging (PCI) were performed with an X-ray beam size of 40 nm at 17 KeV energy (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is a technical specification of the synchrotron imaging method.

claim: Nano-SXRF, PCI, and STED microscopy images can be merged to perform multimodal correlative microscopy of chemical elements, electron density, and fluorescently labeled proteins all obtained at similar spatial resolution (<40 nm).
source: Nano-SXRF, PCI, and STED microscopy images can be merged to perform multimodal correlative microscopy (Figure 1c) of chemical elements, electron density, and fluorescently labeled proteins all obtained at similar spatial resolution (<40 nm).
evidence: This describes the capability of the correlative imaging approach.

claim: Post-acquisition alignment of multimodal images was performed using intra-specimen localization structures such as characteristic filament crosses or dendritic protrusions.
source: Post-acquisition alignment of the multimodal images was performed using intra-specimen localization structures such as characteristic filament crosses, or dendritic protrusions.
evidence: This describes the image alignment methodology.

claim: The post-acquisition alignment result is accurate despite the freeze-drying process that can marginally alter the cell structure.
source: The result is accurate despite the freeze-drying process that can marginally alter the cell structure (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is an assessment of the alignment accuracy.

claim: The adequacy of sample preparation and post-acquisition alignment was checked by comparing live-cell STED with STXM of freeze-dried cells obtained with 25 nm spatial resolution.
source: The adequacy of the sample preparation method and of the post-acquisition alignment of the images for the correlative purpose was checked by comparing live-cell STED with STXM (Scanning Transmission X-ray Microscopy) of freeze-dried cells obtained with 25 nm spatial resolution at HERMES beamline, SOLEIL synchrotron.
evidence: This describes a validation experiment.

claim: STXM enabled visualization of dendritic morphology showing exact superposition of dendrites after cryofixation and freeze-drying with SiR-tubulin fluorescence previously observed by STED on living cells.
source: STXM enabled to visualize the dendritic morphology showing the exact superposition of dendrites after cryofixation and freeze- drying with SiR-tubulin fluorescence previously observed by STED on living cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a validation result showing preservation of structure.

claim: The limit of detection for zinc in nano-SXRF analysis is 0.009 ng.mm−2, corresponding to 14 zeptogram of zinc (about 130 atoms) per pixel of 40 nm x 40 nm size.
source: The limit of detection (LOD) of nano-SXRF analysis was calculated for the detected elements according to IUPAC (International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry) guideline resulting for zinc in in a 0.009 ng.mm−2 LOD, corresponding to 14 zeptogram of zinc (about 130 atoms) per pixel of 40 nm x 40 nm size (Table 1).
evidence: This is a technical specification of the analytical sensitivity.

claim: The highest zinc content is found in F-actin-rich dendritic spines.
source: The highest zinc content is found in F-actin-rich dendritic spines where zinc is highly correlated with sulfur (Person's correlation coefficient >0.6) (Figures 2–4 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the nano-SXRF imaging.

claim: Zinc is highly correlated with sulfur in F-actin-rich dendritic spines (Pearson's correlation coefficient >0.6).
source: The highest zinc content is found in F-actin-rich dendritic spines where zinc is highly correlated with sulfur (Person's correlation coefficient >0.6) (Figures 2–4 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from correlation analysis of imaging data.

claim: Zinc distribution is not fully superimposed with F-actin localization.
source: Zinc distribution however is not fully superimposed with F-actin localization suggesting that both entities are not directly in interaction in dendritic protrusions.
evidence: This is an observation from the correlative imaging.

claim: Zinc and F-actin are not directly in interaction in dendritic protrusions.
source: Zinc distribution however is not fully superimposed with F-actin localization suggesting that both entities are not directly in interaction in dendritic protrusions.
evidence: This is an inference from the partial co-localization observed.

claim: Zinc and sulfur hot spots are found within narrow regions in dendritic spines characterized by the highest electron densities as shown by synchrotron PCI maps.
source: Zinc and sulfur hot spots are found within narrow regions in the dendritic spines characterized by the highest electron densities as shown by synchrotron PCI maps (Figure 3 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from correlating SXRF with PCI imaging.

claim: Copper was detected in F-actin-rich dendritic spines showing a distinct distribution pattern than zinc.
source: Although in lower concentration than zinc, copper was also detected in F-actin-rich dendritic spines showing a distinct distribution pattern than for Zn (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the nano-SXRF imaging.

claim: Copper concentration in dendritic spines is lower than zinc concentration.
source: Although in lower concentration than zinc, copper was also detected in F-actin-rich dendritic spines showing a distinct distribution pattern than for Zn (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison from the imaging data.

claim: Copper is mainly located at the basis of dendritic protrusions.
source: Copper is mainly located at the basis of the dendritic protrusions (Figure 3h) where it is co-localized with the highest fluorescence signal of F-actin (Figure 3j).
evidence: This is a finding from the correlative imaging.

claim: Copper is co-localized with the highest fluorescence signal of F-actin at the basis of dendritic protrusions.
source: Copper is mainly located at the basis of the dendritic protrusions (Figure 3h) where it is co-localized with the highest fluorescence signal of F-actin (Figure 3j).
evidence: This is a finding from the correlative imaging.

claim: The co-localization of copper and F-actin in dendritic protrusions is only partial since copper may not be detected in regions of weaker SiR-actin fluorescence.
source: The co-localization of copper and F-actin in dendritic protrusions is only partial since copper may not be detected in regions of weaker SiR-actin fluorescence.
evidence: This is an observation from the correlative imaging.

claim: In rare cases iron was detected as 200 nm x 100 nm structures of locally dense iron spots in the dendrite, contiguous to the dendritic spines.
source: In rare cases iron was also detected, as 200 nm x 100 nm structures of locally dense iron spots, in the dendrite, contiguous to the dendritic spines (Figure 4—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: This is a finding from the nano-SXRF imaging.

claim: Zinc and tubulin are co-localized in thin dendritic processes.
source: The most striking result of this correlative microscopy approach is the observation of zinc and tubulin co-localization in thin dendritic processes as illustrated in Figures 4–5 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 1.
evidence: This is described as the most striking primary finding.

claim: Parallel tubulin filaments could not be resolved by confocal microscopy but only by STED microscopy.
source: These parallel tubulin filaments could not be resolved by confocal microscopy (Figure 5b), but only by STED microscopy (Figure 5c).
evidence: This demonstrates the superior resolution of STED over confocal microscopy.

claim: Nano-SXRF performed on parallel microtubule filaments was able to separate the element distributions of two thin dendritic processes, similarly to STED microscopy.
source: Similarly to STED microscopy, nano-SXRF performed on the same roi was able to separate the element distributions of the two thin dendritic processes (Figure 5d–e).
evidence: This demonstrates the comparable spatial resolution of nano-SXRF to STED.

claim: Plot profiles of zinc and tubulin relative signal intensities across two tubulin filaments show co-localization of their distributions.
source: Plot profiles of zinc and tubulin relative signal intensities across the two tubulin filaments shows the co-localization of their distributions (Figure 5f).
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis showing co-localization.

claim: The superimposition of S and Zn distributions along tubulin imaged by STED is systematically observed.
source: The very good superimposition of S and Zn distributions along tubulin imaged by STED is systematically observed (Figures 4 and 5k and Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a consistent observation across multiple samples.

claim: For thinner dendrites, zinc is superimposed with the dendritic structure.
source: For thinner dendrites, zinc is superimposed with the dendritic structure, while for thicker branches zinc is located in sub-dendritic regions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation about zinc distribution in different dendrite sizes.

claim: For thicker dendritic branches, zinc is located in sub-dendritic regions.
source: For thinner dendrites, zinc is superimposed with the dendritic structure, while for thicker branches zinc is located in sub-dendritic regions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation about zinc distribution in different dendrite sizes.

claim: The atomic ratio S/Zn in regions showing Zn and tubulin co-localization is 43 ± 11.
source: The quantitative analysis of nano-SXRF data for 21 regions showing Zn and tubulin co-localization indicates that the atomic ratio S/Zn is of 43 ± 11 (Figure 5l and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from analysis of 21 regions.

claim: The amino acid sequence of rat tubulin-α/β dimer contains 49 sulfur atoms per dimer from methionine and cysteine residues.
source: Considering that the amino acid sequence of the rat tubulin-α/β dimer contains 49 sulfur atoms per dimer, from methionine and cysteine residues, the S/Zn ratio in microtubules corresponds to a theoretical tubulin-α/β dimer over Zn ratio of 0.9 ± 0.2 (Figure 5l).
evidence: This is based on known protein sequence information.

claim: The S/Zn ratio in microtubules corresponds to a theoretical tubulin-α/β dimer over Zn ratio of 0.9 ± 0.2.
source: Considering that the amino acid sequence of the rat tubulin-α/β dimer contains 49 sulfur atoms per dimer, from methionine and cysteine residues, the S/Zn ratio in microtubules corresponds to a theoretical tubulin-α/β dimer over Zn ratio of 0.9 ± 0.2 (Figure 5l).
evidence: This is calculated from the measured S/Zn ratio and known protein composition.

claim: Primary rat hippocampal neurons were exposed to TPEN, a zinc intracellular chelator.
source: Primary rat hippocampal neurons cultured on glass coverslips were exposed to TPEN (N,N,N',N'-tetrakis(2-pyridylmethyl)ethylenediamine), a zinc intracellular chelator.
evidence: This describes the experimental treatment.

claim: Mature neurons at DIV 15 were exposed to a subcytotoxic concentration of 5 µM TPEN during 24 hr.
source: At DIV 15, mature neurons were exposed to a subcytotoxic concentration of 5 µM TPEN during 24 hr, or simultaneously to 5 µM TPEN and 10 µM ZnCl2, or to 0.1% ethanol (v/v) for the control group.
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions.

claim: Subcytotoxic concentration of TPEN during 24 hr exposure was selected to study the effect of mild zinc depletion conditions on neuronal differentiation, avoiding cytoskeleton alteration from direct cytotoxic effects at higher TPEN concentrations.
source: Subcytotoxic concentration of TPEN during 24 hr exposure time was selected to study the effect of mild zinc depletion conditions on neuronal differentiation, avoiding cytoskeleton alteration that would result from direct cytotoxic effects at higher TPEN concentrations.
evidence: This explains the rationale for the chosen experimental conditions.

claim: Zinc chelation with 5 µM TPEN results in a statistically significant decrease of β-tubulin fluorescence compared to the control group.
source: Zinc chelation with 5 µM TPEN results in a statistically significant decrease of β-tubulin and F-actin fluorescence compared to the control group (Figure 6d–e and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the quantitative fluorescence microscopy experiments.

claim: Zinc chelation with 5 µM TPEN results in a statistically significant decrease of F-actin fluorescence compared to the control group.
source: Zinc chelation with 5 µM TPEN results in a statistically significant decrease of β-tubulin and F-actin fluorescence compared to the control group (Figure 6d–e and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the quantitative fluorescence microscopy experiments.

claim: The decrease in β-tubulin and F-actin expression following TPEN exposure is reversed by the addition of Zn.
source: The decrease in β-tubulin and F-actin expression following TPEN exposure is reversed by the addition of Zn strongly suggesting that the effect of TPEN is due to Zn chelation and not to unspecific interactions (Figure 6d–e and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the rescue experiment.

claim: The effect of TPEN is due to Zn chelation and not to unspecific interactions.
source: The decrease in β-tubulin and F-actin expression following TPEN exposure is reversed by the addition of Zn strongly suggesting that the effect of TPEN is due to Zn chelation and not to unspecific interactions (Figure 6d–e and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference from the rescue experiment showing specificity.

claim: STED microscopy has been successfully combined with transmission electron microscopy to correlate protein localization with cell ultrastructure.
source: STED microscopy has already been successfully combined to transmission electron microscopy to correlate protein localization with cell ultrastructure (Watanabe et al., 2011), or to atomic force microscopy to investigate protein aggregation at high spatial resolution (Cosentino et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge about prior correlative microscopy approaches.

claim: STED microscopy has been successfully combined with atomic force microscopy to investigate protein aggregation at high spatial resolution.
source: STED microscopy has already been successfully combined to transmission electron microscopy to correlate protein localization with cell ultrastructure (Watanabe et al., 2011), or to atomic force microscopy to investigate protein aggregation at high spatial resolution (Cosentino et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge about prior correlative microscopy approaches.

claim: STED has been performed together with synchrotron scanning diffraction microscopy to inform about diffraction patterns in cells.
source: Recently, STED has been performed together with synchrotron scanning diffraction microscopy to inform about diffraction patterns in cells (Bernhardt et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge about prior correlative microscopy approaches.

claim: Previous correlative approaches cannot be transposed to imaging of metals in cells since they require chemical fixation known to disrupt metal-binding equilibrium in cells.
source: These correlative approaches however cannot be transposed to the imaging of metals in cells since they require steps of chemical fixation known to disrupt the metal-binding equilibrium in cells (Roudeau et al., 2014; Perrin et al., 2015).
evidence: This explains a limitation of prior approaches for metal imaging.

claim: Glass coverslips used for STED microscopy usually contain significant amounts of zinc and some other trace metals.
source: Moreover, glass coverslips used for STED microscopy usually contain significant amounts of zinc and of some other trace metals.
evidence: This is a practical consideration for metal imaging experiments.

claim: The protocol combines high-resolution imaging (40 nm) and high elemental sensitivity (zeptogram level).
source: Our protocol combines high-resolution imaging (40 nm) and high elemental sensitivity (zeptogram level).
evidence: This describes the capabilities of the developed method.

claim: The investigations focused on metal interactions with F-actin and tubulin based on previous SXRF nano-imaging results.
source: We focused our investigations on metal interactions with two cytoskeleton proteins, F-actin and tubulin based on our previous SXRF nano-imaging results showing the localization of zinc in dendritic shafts and of copper in the spines of hippocampal neurons (Perrin et al., 2017).
evidence: This explains the rationale for the choice of proteins to study.

claim: Zinc is present in different regions of the brain, mainly the hippocampus and the amygdala.
source: Zinc is present in different regions of the brain, mainly the hippocampus and the amygdala (Frederickson et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge about zinc distribution in the brain.

claim: Zinc is largely complexed to proteins and is required for the functioning of hundreds of proteins.
source: Zinc is largely complexed to proteins and is required for the functioning of hundreds of proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge about zinc biochemistry.

claim: Only 10% of the total zinc is in a labile state, often referred as zinc ions (Zn2+).
source: Only 10% of the total zinc is in a labile state, often referred as zinc ions (Zn2+), a more easily exchangeable and therefore mobile element pool (Takeda, 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge about zinc speciation in cells.

claim: Labile zinc is a more easily exchangeable and therefore mobile element pool.
source: Only 10% of the total zinc is in a labile state, often referred as zinc ions (Zn2+), a more easily exchangeable and therefore mobile element pool (Takeda, 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the properties of labile zinc.

claim: Zinc is released in the synaptic cleft where it inhibits neuronal transmission mediated by AMPARs or NMDARs.
source: As for other neurotransmitters, zinc is released in the synaptic cleft where it inhibits neuronal transmission mediated by AMPARs or NMDARs (Vergnano et al., 2014; Barr and Burdette, 2017; Kalappa et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about zinc function in synaptic transmission.

claim: Zinc dyshomeostasis is broadly associated with brain diseases such as age-related cognitive decline, depression, or Alzheimer's disease.
source: Zinc dyshomeostasis is broadly associated to brain diseases such as age-related cognitive decline, depression, or Alzheimer's disease (Portbury and Adlard, 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge about zinc in disease.

claim: The highest zinc content in dendritic spines is mainly located at the head of the spines.
source: The highest zinc content is found in dendritic spines, mainly located at the head of the spines, and zinc distribution was correlated with the higher cellular density as shown by synchrotron PCI.
evidence: This is a finding from the imaging experiments.

claim: Zinc distribution in dendritic spines is correlated with higher cellular density as shown by synchrotron PCI.
source: The highest zinc content is found in dendritic spines, mainly located at the head of the spines, and zinc distribution was correlated with the higher cellular density as shown by synchrotron PCI.
evidence: This is a finding from correlating SXRF with PCI.

claim: The result of zinc localization at spine heads is in agreement with the expected location of zinc in the postsynaptic density (PSD) of hippocampal synapses.
source: This result is in agreement with the expected location of zinc in the postsynaptic density (PSD) of hippocampal synapses where zinc could play a structural function in stabilizing proteins associated to the PSD such as Shank3 (Tao-Cheng et al., 2016).
evidence: This connects the finding to established knowledge about synaptic structure.

claim: Zinc could play a structural function in stabilizing proteins associated to the PSD such as Shank3.
source: This result is in agreement with the expected location of zinc in the postsynaptic density (PSD) of hippocampal synapses where zinc could play a structural function in stabilizing proteins associated to the PSD such as Shank3 (Tao-Cheng et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citation.

claim: Zinc co-localization with microtubules results in a stoichiometry of 0.9 ± 0.2 zinc atom per tubulin-αβ dimer based on the known amino acid composition of neuronal rat tubulin-αβ dimer.
source: Based on the known amino acid composition of neuronal rat tubulin-αβ dimer, zinc co-localization with microtubules results in a stoichiometry of 0.9 ± 0.2 zinc atom per tubulin-αβ dimer.
evidence: This is a calculated result from the imaging data and known protein composition.

claim: The result of 0.9 ± 0.2 zinc atom per tubulin-αβ dimer is in excellent agreement with data obtained by the Scatchard method on purified microtubule preparations from pig brains showing 0.86 ± 0.18 zinc atom per tubulin-αβ dimer.
source: This result is in excellent agreement with data obtained by the Scatchard method on purified microtubule preparations from pig brains showing that zinc could bind tubulin with a molecular ratio of 0.86 ± 0.18 zinc atom per tubulin-αβ dimer (Hesketh, 1983).
evidence: This compares the current finding with prior biochemical measurements.

claim: The Scatchard method consists in measuring the affinity of tubulin for zinc ions by adding known quantities of zinc to the purified protein.
source: The Scatchard method consists in measuring the affinity of tubulin for zinc ions by adding known quantities of zinc to the purified protein.
evidence: This explains the Scatchard method.

claim: The result is in agreement with X-ray crystallography data of the tubulin-α/β dimer predicting the presence of one putative zinc ion per dimer, located in the tubulin-α subunit of zinc-induced tubulin sheets.
source: Our result is also in agreement with X-ray crystallography data of the tubulin-α/β dimer predicting the presence of one putative zinc ion per dimer, located in the tubulin-α subunit of zinc-induced tubulin sheets (Löwe et al., 2001).
evidence: This compares the current finding with structural biology data.

claim: Molecular modeling has identified six putative binding sites of zinc to tubulin.
source: Moreover, molecular modeling have identified six putative binding sites of zinc to tubulin, suggesting that zinc would stabilize the structure of microtubules by enhancing electrostatic interactions (Craddock et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge from computational studies.

claim: Zinc would stabilize the structure of microtubules by enhancing electrostatic interactions.
source: Moreover, molecular modeling have identified six putative binding sites of zinc to tubulin, suggesting that zinc would stabilize the structure of microtubules by enhancing electrostatic interactions (Craddock et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from molecular modeling studies.

claim: The imaging approach cannot prove a direct interaction between zinc and tubulin.
source: Although our imaging approach cannot prove a direct interaction between zinc and tubulin, our data were obtained directly on primary cultured neurons in physiological conditions, without zinc addition, supporting the hypothesis of a structural requirement for zinc in tubulin network assembly.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the imaging method.

claim: The data were obtained directly on primary cultured neurons in physiological conditions, without zinc addition.
source: Although our imaging approach cannot prove a direct interaction between zinc and tubulin, our data were obtained directly on primary cultured neurons in physiological conditions, without zinc addition, supporting the hypothesis of a structural requirement for zinc in tubulin network assembly.
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions.

claim: The data support the hypothesis of a structural requirement for zinc in tubulin network assembly.
source: Although our imaging approach cannot prove a direct interaction between zinc and tubulin, our data were obtained directly on primary cultured neurons in physiological conditions, without zinc addition, supporting the hypothesis of a structural requirement for zinc in tubulin network assembly.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: It has been hypothesized that zinc dyshomeostasis could alter tubulin dynamics.
source: It has been hypothesized that zinc dyshomeostasis could alter tubulin dynamics (Craddock et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from prior literature.

claim: The hypothesis that zinc dyshomeostasis could alter tubulin dynamics is supported by the reduction of the neuronal cytoskeleton induced by zinc depletion using TPEN.
source: In our study, this hypothesis is supported by the reduction of the neuronal cytoskeleton induced by zinc depletion using the intracellular zinc-chelator TPEN.
evidence: This connects the TPEN experiments to the hypothesis.

claim: TPEN exposure resulted in decreased tubulin expression and this effect was reversed by Zn.
source: We found that TPEN exposure resulted in decreased tubulin expression and that this effect was reversed by Zn.
evidence: This is a finding from the TPEN experiments.

claim: The decrease in tubulin expression can be explained by limited neuronal differentiation resulting in reduced density of tubulin filaments.
source: The decrease in tubulin expression can be explained by a limited neuronal differentiation resulting in a reduced density of tubulin filaments.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the TPEN results.

claim: A concomitant decrease of F-actin expression was observed with tubulin decrease.
source: We also observe a concomitant decrease of F-actin expression that could be explained as the consequence of tubulin decrease since microtubules are involved in the regulation of dendritic spines through actin remodeling (Jaworski et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a finding from the TPEN experiments.

claim: The decrease of F-actin expression could be explained as the consequence of tubulin decrease since microtubules are involved in the regulation of dendritic spines through actin remodeling.
source: We also observe a concomitant decrease of F-actin expression that could be explained as the consequence of tubulin decrease since microtubules are involved in the regulation of dendritic spines through actin remodeling (Jaworski et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting the findings to established knowledge.

claim: The zinc chelation results are in agreement with previous observations that zinc supplementation in culture medium induces increase of β-tubulin and F-actin expression in mature primary rat hippocampal neurons.
source: These zinc chelation results are in agreement with our previous observation that zinc supplementation in the culture medium induces the increase of β-tubulin and F-actin expression in mature primary rat hippocampal neurons (Perrin et al., 2017).
evidence: This connects the current findings to prior work by the authors.

claim: Copper is an essential metal for various cellular functions such as respiration, defense against free radicals and neurotransmitter synthesis.
source: Copper is an essential metal for various cellular functions such as respiration, defense against free radicals and neurotransmitter synthesis (Chang, 2015; D'Ambrosi and Rossi, 2015; Xiao et al., 2018; Hatori et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge about copper functions.

claim: Contrary to zinc ions, copper is not localized within synaptic vesicles.
source: Contrary to zinc ions, copper is not localized within synaptic vesicles but copper ions can be released into the synaptic cleft by means of copper transporter proteins (D'Ambrosi and Rossi, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about copper localization.

claim: Copper ions can be released into the synaptic cleft by means of copper transporter proteins.
source: Contrary to zinc ions, copper is not localized within synaptic vesicles but copper ions can be released into the synaptic cleft by means of copper transporter proteins (D'Ambrosi and Rossi, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about copper release mechanisms.

claim: Copper can play a biphasic role on neural transmission mediated by AMPARs, either by blocking or increasing neurotransmission depending on its concentration and time of exposure.
source: Copper can play a biphasic role on neural transmission mediated by AMPARs, either by blocking or increasing the neurotransmission depending on its concentration and time of exposure (Peters et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge about copper effects on neurotransmission.

claim: Disturbed copper homeostasis is found in many neurological diseases.
source: As for zinc, a disturbed copper homeostasis is found in many neurological diseases (D'Ambrosi and Rossi, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about copper in disease.

claim: Copper deficiency is observed in brain regions targeted for neurodegeneration such as the substantia nigra in Parkinson's disease.
source: Copper deficiency is observed in brain regions targeted for neurodegeneration such as the substantia nigra in Parkinson's disease (Davies et al., 2014), or the hippocampus in Alzheimer's disease (Xu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge about copper deficiency in disease.

claim: Copper deficiency is observed in the hippocampus in Alzheimer's disease.
source: Copper deficiency is observed in brain regions targeted for neurodegeneration such as the substantia nigra in Parkinson's disease (Davies et al., 2014), or the hippocampus in Alzheimer's disease (Xu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge about copper deficiency in disease.

claim: The data highlight the specific localization of copper within F-actin-rich regions along dendrites.
source: Our data highlight the specific localization of copper within F-actin-rich regions along dendrites.
evidence: This is a summary of the copper localization findings.

claim: The position, size and shape of F-actin protrusions observed by STED microscopy are representative of dendritic spines.
source: The position, size and shape of the F-actin protrusions observed by STED microscopy (Figure 2 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 1) are representative of dendritic spines (Chazeau and Giannone, 2016; Sala and Segal, 2014).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on morphological characteristics and citations.

claim: Actin-rich structures may include actin patches in addition to dendritic spines.
source: Although actin-rich structures should predominantly be components of dendritic spines, other actin-rich structures may be present such as actin patches (Konietzny et al., 2017).
evidence: This acknowledges other possible structures based on literature.

claim: Both dendritic spines and actin patches are important triggers of synaptic differentiation.
source: Both dendritic spines and actin patches are important triggers of synaptic differentiation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about these structures.

claim: Copper might bind directly to F-actin but copper content is below the detection limit in regions containing lower amount of F-actin.
source: This observation could be explained by two different mechanisms. Copper might bind directly to F-actin but copper content is below the detection limit in regions containing lower amount of F-actin.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the partial co-localization.

claim: Copper might not bind directly to F-actin but rather to other potential Cu-binding biomolecules that can interact with F-actin in specific areas of dendritic protrusions where F-actin content is high.
source: Copper might not bind directly to F-actin but rather to other potential Cu-binding biomolecules that can interact with F-actin in specific areas of the dendritic protrusions where F-actin content is high.
evidence: This is an alternative speculative explanation for the partial co-localization.

claim: In an IMAC study focused on the copper proteome of HepG2 cells, γ-actin was identified as displaying Cu-binding ability in both microsomal and cytosolic fractions.
source: In an IMAC study focused on the copper proteome of HepG2 cells, 48 cytosolic proteins and 19 microsomal proteins displayed Cu-binding ability, among them γ-actin was identified both in the microsomal and the cytosolic fractions (Smith et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge from a prior proteomics study.

claim: Since γ-actin is highly expressed in neurons, the IMAC result could suggest a direct binding of copper to F-actin in hippocampal neurons.
source: Since γ-actin is also highly expressed in neurons, this IMAC result could suggest a direct binding of copper to F-actin in hippocampal neurons as well.
evidence: This is a speculative inference from prior proteomics data.

claim: Cofilin was identified as a putative Cu-binding protein in the cytosolic fraction in the IMAC study.
source: In this same study, cofilin was also identified as putative Cu-binding protein in the cytosolic fraction (Smith et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge from a prior proteomics study.

claim: Copper could interact indirectly with molecules involved in the regulation of F-actin network in the dendritic spine such as cofilin, explaining the partial co-localization with F-actin.
source: Copper could interact indirectly with molecules involved in the regulation of F-actin network in the dendritic spine such as cofilin, explaining the partial co-localization with F-actin.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the partial co-localization.

claim: Iron was not detected within dendritic spines.
source: It is interesting to underline that iron was not detected within dendritic spines, meaning that iron content in this compartment is below the detection limit of the method, suggesting that contrary to copper and zinc, iron is probably not directly involved in the morphogenesis of the dendritic spines.
evidence: This is a finding from the nano-SXRF imaging.

claim: Iron content in dendritic spines is below the detection limit of the method.
source: It is interesting to underline that iron was not detected within dendritic spines, meaning that iron content in this compartment is below the detection limit of the method, suggesting that contrary to copper and zinc, iron is probably not directly involved in the morphogenesis of the dendritic spines.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the non-detection of iron.

claim: Contrary to copper and zinc, iron is probably not directly involved in the morphogenesis of dendritic spines.
source: It is interesting to underline that iron was not detected within dendritic spines, meaning that iron content in this compartment is below the detection limit of the method, suggesting that contrary to copper and zinc, iron is probably not directly involved in the morphogenesis of the dendritic spines.
evidence: This is an inference from the absence of iron detection in spines.

claim: Iron was observed as local hot spots of few hundred nanometers along dendrites.
source: On the other hand, iron was observed as local hot spots of few hundred of nanometers along dendrites, the exact nature of these local iron-enrichment remains to be elucidated.
evidence: This is a finding from the nano-SXRF imaging.

claim: The exact nature of local iron-enrichment along dendrites remains to be elucidated.
source: On the other hand, iron was observed as local hot spots of few hundred of nanometers along dendrites, the exact nature of these local iron-enrichment remains to be elucidated.
evidence: This acknowledges an unanswered question.

claim: A possible explanation for local iron-enrichment could be the presence of iron in mitochondria known to be present in dendrites of hippocampal neurons.
source: A possible explanation could be the presence of iron in mitochondria known to be present in dendrites of hippocampal neurons (Bastian et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation based on known biology.

claim: The combination of STED super-resolution microscopy and nano-SXRF imaging stands as a solid new tool for the identification of metalloproteins directly in cells by correlating cellular imaging methods at a supramolecular scale.
source: From a methodological perspective, the combination of STED super-resolution microscopy and nano-SXRF imaging stands as a solid new tool for the identification of metalloproteins directly in cells by correlating cellular imaging methods at a supramolecular scale.
evidence: This is a statement about the methodological contribution of the work.

claim: The correlative imaging approach revealed the co-segregation of zinc and copper with respectively microtubules and F-actin.
source: This correlative imaging approach revealed the co-segregation of zinc and copper with respectively microtubules and F-actin.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: Further experiments are required to elucidate the interaction mechanisms between these metals and the cytoskeleton architecture.
source: Further experiments are now required to elucidate the interaction mechanisms between these metals and the cytoskeleton architecture.
evidence: This is a statement about future research needs.

claim: Given the importance of cytoskeleton proteins in the morphological plasticity of neuronal connections, the results may contribute to explain why copper and zinc are present in higher concentrations in the nervous system than in other organs.
source: Finally, given the importance of cytoskeleton proteins in the morphological plasticity of neuronal connections (Sala and Segal, 2014), our results may contribute to explain why copper and zinc are present in higher concentrations in the nervous system than in other organs.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the findings to broader biological significance.
